Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Networking & Multiplayer Basics
Networking & Multiplayer Basics
Understand authority, replication, and RPCs to synchronize gameplay across machines.

Why this matters: Multiplayer introduces authority boundaries. Making the right replication and RPC choices prevents desyncs and cheating.

Concrete outcome: You will implement a replicated health component and a multicast damage effect that logs on both server and clients.

In this lesson
Client-server model, replication, RPCs, implementing replicated variables, testing with editor instances.
Model
Client-Server
Server is authoritative. Clients send input and receive replicated state.
Mechanic
Replication & RPCs
Variables marked with UPROPERTY(Replicated) and Remote Procedure Calls synchronize state and events.
Explore Key Topics
Client-Server Model
Server holds authoritative state; clients simulate and send input.
Replication
Mark what must be shared with UPROPERTY and GetLifetimeReplicatedProps.
RPCs
Use Server, Client, and NetMulticast for remote execution of functions.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: This first objective set explains the core skills you will practice and why they matter. You will learn to explain the client-server architecture used by Unreal Engine. That means identifying authority, ownership, and the role of the server as the authoritative source of game state. You will also understand replication — how variables and properties travel from server to clients — and why explicit marking and lifetime registration is required. Practically, you will implement variable replication using the UPROPERTY(Replicated) specifier and by overriding GetLifetimeReplicatedProps with DOREPLIFETIME entries. These are essential steps to make a player’s health or inventory visible to other players without leaking private data. Finally, you will learn to distinguish and implement Server, Client, and NetMulticast RPCs, choosing which remote call fits a given gameplay need. Each of these skills is tied to preventing cheating, conserving bandwidth, and keeping gameplay consistent, and you will see small code examples and a hands-on health component task as practice.

screens.title: Client-Server Architecture
screens.narratorSegment: A clear definition first: in Unreal Engine multiplayer the game commonly runs in a client-server architecture where the server holds the authoritative game state and clients are responsible for local input and simulation. That means the server validates and applies changes like movement, item pickups, or damage, and then replicates resulting state back to clients. A concrete example is firing a weapon: the client requests the fire action, but the server applies damage and updates the target's health so all clients observe a single consistent outcome. A common misconception is to treat clients as equal peers; doing so opens doors for cheating and unpredictable desynchronization. Another pitfall is assuming the server does no rendering work — a listen server may also render locally, but authority still comes from server logic. Why this matters in practice: understanding authority helps you decide where to put code — input validation on the server, local cosmetic effects on clients, and replicated state on the server for distribution. As you design gameplay, ask: which side must be authoritative for fair and consistent outcomes? Client-Server Architecture means treat the server as the final arbiter of game logic; clients send input and receive authoritative state to stay consistent.. In practical terms, authority, ownership, and the server as source of truth. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Client-Server Architecture
Definition

Server holds authoritative game state; clients send input and simulate until the server confirms.

Concrete example
Client requests fire, server validates and applies damage, then replicates updated health so everyone sees the same result.
Common misconception
Treating clients as equal authority causes security and consistency problems; always decide which side must validate actions.
Why it matters
Authority decisions determine where to implement core gameplay checks and how to communicate results to clients reliably.
Scenario & Takeaway
Imagine a pickup action: the client asks to pick an item, but the server confirms availability and then tells every client to remove it. Implement pickup logic on the server to prevent duplicated pickups or cheating.
Key Takeaway

Always place authoritative checks on the server and use replication to distribute the resulting state to clients.

screens.title: Replication Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: Replication is the engine feature that synchronizes variables, properties, and function calls from the server to clients. In practical terms, you mark a variable with UPROPERTY(Replicated) and then register it in GetLifetimeReplicatedProps so the engine knows to send it. A concrete example is a player's CurrentHealth: the server changes it, and the engine sends that updated value to all clients who should see it. Unreal also supports RepNotify by using ReplicatedUsing to trigger an OnRep function on clients when a value arrives; this is useful for updating a HUD or local effects. A frequent misconception is that marking a variable as Replicated alone is sufficient—without adding it to GetLifetimeReplicatedProps the engine won't replicate it. Another subtlety is replication conditions, like COND_OwnerOnly, which let you limit who receives data — useful for private inventories or owner-only UI. Understanding replication gives you fine-grained control over bandwidth, privacy, and client experience. Replication Fundamentals means mark variables with uproperty(replicated) and register them in getlifetimereplicatedprops to ensure the engine synchronizes them.. In practical terms, how unreal synchronizes variables and events. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Replication rule
keyIdea.text: Mark variables with UPROPERTY(Replicated) and register them in GetLifetimeReplicatedProps to ensure the engine synchronizes them.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Replication Fundamentals
Key steps
  • 1. Use UPROPERTY(Replicated) on variables that must travel to clients.
  • 2. Override GetLifetimeReplicatedProps and call DOREPLIFETIME for each property.
  • 3. Optionally use ReplicatedUsing to run an OnRep callback on clients.
  • 4. Use replication conditions to restrict who receives data.
Common mistake
Adding Replicated without DOREPLIFETIME: the engine will not actually send updates unless the property is registered for lifetime replication.
Example: GetLifetimeReplicatedProps
// In MyHealthComponent.cpp
void UMyHealthComponent::GetLifetimeReplicatedProps(TArray<FLifetimeProperty>& OutLifetimeProps) const
{
  Super::GetLifetimeReplicatedProps(OutLifetimeProps);
  DOREPLIFETIME(UMyHealthComponent, CurrentHealth);
}
This registration tells Unreal which properties to watch and send to clients. Use conditions like COND_OwnerOnly when data should be private to the owning player.
Key Takeaway

Replication requires both marking and registration; OnRep callbacks let clients react when values arrive.

screens.title: RPC Types: Server, Client, NetMulticast
screens.narratorSegment: Remote Procedure Calls let you execute logic on a remote machine. There are three main types you must know. Server RPCs are called by a client and executed on the server; use them for input that must be validated and applied authoritatively, for example asking the server to apply damage. Client RPCs are called by the server and executed on a single owning client; they are ideal for client-specific feedback like showing a unique UI or playing a local sound. NetMulticast RPCs are called by the server and executed on all clients and the server itself — use them for global visual or audio effects, such as playing an explosion animation everyone should see. A concrete example: when damage occurs, the client asks the server to apply damage via a Server RPC; the server updates health and calls a NetMulticast RPC to play the damage effect for every player. A common mistake is attempting to call a Server RPC from a non-owning client or calling Client RPCs from a client; RPCs must originate from the correct authority and actor ownership.

keyIdea.text: Server for authoritative requests, Client for owner-only feedback, NetMulticast for global effects.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › RPC Types
Server RPC
Called by a client, runs on the server. Use for validated, authoritative actions like ApplyDamage. Mark Reliable if arrival matters and WithValidation for custom checks.
Client RPC
Called by server, runs only on the owning client. Use for owner-specific UI updates or sounds.
NetMulticast RPC
Called by server, runs on all clients and server. Use for global effects like explosions or shared animations.
Concrete code examples
// Server RPC
UFUNCTION(Server, Reliable, WithValidation)
void Server_ApplyDamage(float DamageAmount);

// Client RPC
UFUNCTION(Client, Reliable)
void Client_DisplayHitMarker();

// NetMulticast RPC
UFUNCTION(NetMulticast, Reliable)
void Multicast_PlayDamageEffect();
Pitfall
RPCs must originate from correct authority and owning actor. Calling Server RPCs from non-owning clients silently fails.
Key Takeaway

Match RPC type to intent: validation on server, owner feedback on client, shared visual effects via multicast.

screens.title: Implementing Variable Replication
screens.narratorSegment: Implementing replication has a small set of repeatable steps you will perform in C++. First, decide which variables must be shared. Mark each with UPROPERTY(Replicated) or UPROPERTY(ReplicatedUsing=OnRep_Function) when you want a client callback. Second, set bReplicates = true in your actor or ensure the component is attached to a replicated actor. Third, override GetLifetimeReplicatedProps and call DOREPLIFETIME for every variable you marked. Fourth, when required, implement an OnRep function to respond to changes on clients, for example updating UI or broadcasting delegates for local systems. A concrete example: CurrentHealth is a float marked with ReplicatedUsing=OnRep_CurrentHealth; the server modifies CurrentHealth, Unreal replicates the value to clients, and the OnRep_CurrentHealth function runs to update the HUD. A common mistake is forgetting to call Super::GetLifetimeReplicatedProps or to include the correct class in DOREPLIFETIME, which prevents replication registration. Follow the process consistently and test with multiple instances to confirm end-to-end replication. Implementing Variable Replication means follow the steps: mark, set replication flags, register with doreplifetime, and use onrep callbacks for client updates.. In practical terms, uproperty(replicated) and getlifetimereplicatedprops in practice. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Implementing Variable Replication
Step-by-step
  1. 1. Mark property: UPROPERTY(Replicated) or ReplicatedUsing=OnRep_Fn.
  2. 2. Ensure actor/component has bReplicates = true.
  3. 3. Override GetLifetimeReplicatedProps and call DOREPLIFETIME(Class, Property).
  4. 4. Implement OnRep to react on clients, update UI or broadcast delegates.
Mistake to avoid
Omitting Super::GetLifetimeReplicatedProps or passing the wrong class to DOREPLIFETIME stops registration.
Concrete code snippet
UPROPERTY(ReplicatedUsing=OnRep_CurrentHealth)
float CurrentHealth;

UFUNCTION()
void OnRep_CurrentHealth();

void UMyHealthComponent::GetLifetimeReplicatedProps(TArray<FLifetimeProperty>& OutLifetimeProps) const
{
  Super::GetLifetimeReplicatedProps(OutLifetimeProps);
  DOREPLIFETIME(UMyHealthComponent, CurrentHealth);
}
This pairing ensures the server-owned CurrentHealth is sent to clients and that they run OnRep_CurrentHealth when the value changes.
Key Takeaway

Register every replicated property for lifetime replication and use OnRep callbacks to react on clients.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Replicated Health Component (Header)
Header excerpt
// MyHealthComponent.h (excerpt)
UPROPERTY(ReplicatedUsing=OnRep_CurrentHealth, VisibleAnywhere, Category="Health")
float CurrentHealth;

UFUNCTION()
void OnRep_CurrentHealth();

UFUNCTION(Server, Reliable, WithValidation)
void Server_ApplyDamage(float DamageAmount);

UFUNCTION(NetMulticast, Reliable)
void Multicast_PlayDamageEffect();

virtual void GetLifetimeReplicatedProps(TArray<FLifetimeProperty>& OutLifetimeProps) const override;
Explanation
  • CurrentHealth: replicated using an OnRep callback for client-side reactions.
  • Server_ApplyDamage: client-to-server request with validation for security.
  • Multicast_PlayDamageEffect: server-triggered visual feedback for all clients.
  • GetLifetimeReplicatedProps: registers CurrentHealth with DOREPLIFETIME.
Pro tip
Keep replication surfaces small: replicate only what you need to reduce bandwidth and complexity.

screens.title: Server_ApplyDamage Implementation
screens.narratorSegment: In this walkthrough we focus on the Server_ApplyDamage RPC implementation. The _Validate function should check that incoming values are plausible and that the caller may perform the action — for the activity it returns true to keep the example simple, but in production you would check cooldowns or ownership. The _Implementation runs on the server: decrease CurrentHealth, clamp it to a minimum, and then call Multicast_PlayDamageEffect so all clients see the effect. Because CurrentHealth is replicated, changing it on the server schedules an update to clients; if you declared ReplicatedUsing, OnRep_CurrentHealth will fire on clients when the new value arrives. A common misconception is expecting OnRep to run on the server; OnRep callbacks run on clients. For the server to see its own state change, call the same local update logic directly on the server after modifying the variable. This pattern ensures all players observe the effect while the server remains the single point of truth for game state. screens.title: bReplicates and Ownership
screens.narratorSegment: Two small flags often cause big headaches: bReplicates and actor ownership. bReplicates = true tells the engine that an actor’s state and RPCs should be considered for networking. If you forget to set this in a constructor, replication and RPC delivery can silently fail. Ownership determines which client can call Server RPCs on an actor; a client can only invoke Server RPCs on actors it owns. For player characters, ownership is usually set automatically, but components or dynamically spawned actors may require explicit ownership handling. A concrete scenario: spawning an item on the server that a client should control — you must set the owner on the server so the client can call RPCs that the server will accept. A common misconception is thinking replication alone grants RPC rights — ownership and authority rules decide whether an RPC call is routed. When in doubt, confirm bReplicates is true and inspect actor roles in logs during testing. bReplicates and Ownership means set breplicates = true and manage ownership so rpcs and replicated properties work as intended.. screens.title: Bandwidth, Privacy, and Replication Conditions
screens.narratorSegment: Not all data should be sent to all players. Replication conditions let you limit who receives a property update. Use COND_OwnerOnly when a piece of data, like a private inventory, should be visible only to its owning client. Restricting replication saves bandwidth and prevents leaking sensitive state. In practice, choose replication for essential gameplay state and prefer local prediction or client-side cosmetic simulation for purely visual elements. A concrete example: replicate an enemy’s health bar to everyone, but replicate a player's inventory only with COND_OwnerOnly. A common mistake is over-replicating complex containers without converting them to compact USTRUCTs or carefully filtering elements; this quickly increases bandwidth costs. Measure and iterate: profile your network traffic, use conditions when appropriate, and keep replication surfaces minimal and explicit. Bandwidth, Privacy, and Replication Conditions means use cond_owneronly and other conditions to limit replication, reduce bandwidth, and protect private data.. In practical terms, use replication conditions to optimize what data goes where. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. When to limit replication

In this lesson you will build a clear mental model of how multiplayer works in Unreal Engine and why replication matters. We start with the client-server architecture — an authoritative server holds the truth while clients send input and simulate predictions. You will see why marking variables for replication and choosing the right RPC type keeps game state consistent and prevents cheating. We’ll also walk through concrete implementation steps: using UPROPERTY(Replicated), overriding GetLifetimeReplicatedProps with DOREPLIFETIME, and writing Server, Client, and NetMulticast RPCs. A short hands-on task will guide you through making a replicated health component and triggering a damage effect for all clients. By the end you’ll be able to reason about authority, ownership, and common pitfalls like forgetting to set bReplicates or calling RPCs from the wrong context. Ready to explore the core topics and practical code patterns that make multiplayer games reliable and debuggable? Keep an eye out for test strategies and simple fixes you can use in everyday development.

This first objective set explains the core skills you will practice and why they matter. You will learn to explain the client-server architecture used by Unreal Engine. That means identifying authority, ownership, and the role of the server as the authoritative source of game state. You will also understand replication — how variables and properties travel from server to clients — and why explicit marking and lifetime registration is required. Practically, you will implement variable replication using the UPROPERTY(Replicated) specifier and by overriding GetLifetimeReplicatedProps with DOREPLIFETIME entries. These are essential steps to make a player’s health or inventory visible to other players without leaking private data. Finally, you will learn to distinguish and implement Server, Client, and NetMulticast RPCs, choosing which remote call fits a given gameplay need. Each of these skills is tied to preventing cheating, conserving bandwidth, and keeping gameplay consistent, and you will see small code examples and a hands-on health component task as practice.

This second objectives screen focuses on implementation and resilience. You will implement Server RPCs with validation and reliable flags so the server processes important client requests like applying damage. You will implement OnRep functions and use ReplicatedUsing to run client-side updates when a replicated variable changes, for example updating a HUD when CurrentHealth arrives. You will learn to set bReplicates = true for actors and components that must be networked — forgetting this is a frequent cause of silent failures. You will also practice testing in the editor with a server and a client instance and reading UE_LOG output to confirm replication and multicast effects. Finally, you will learn to reason about bandwidth and privacy using replication conditions like COND_OwnerOnly to avoid sending inventory data to everyone. Together these objectives turn conceptual knowledge into practical checks you can run while building multiplayer features.

A clear definition first: in Unreal Engine multiplayer the game commonly runs in a client-server architecture where the server holds the authoritative game state and clients are responsible for local input and simulation. That means the server validates and applies changes like movement, item pickups, or damage, and then replicates resulting state back to clients. A concrete example is firing a weapon: the client requests the fire action, but the server applies damage and updates the target's health so all clients observe a single consistent outcome. A common misconception is to treat clients as equal peers; doing so opens doors for cheating and unpredictable desynchronization. Another pitfall is assuming the server does no rendering work — a listen server may also render locally, but authority still comes from server logic. Why this matters in practice: understanding authority helps you decide where to put code — input validation on the server, local cosmetic effects on clients, and replicated state on the server for distribution. As you design gameplay, ask: which side must be authoritative for fair and consistent outcomes? Client-Server Architecture means treat the server as the final arbiter of game logic; clients send input and receive authoritative state to stay consistent.. In practical terms, authority, ownership, and the server as source of truth. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Replication is the engine feature that synchronizes variables, properties, and function calls from the server to clients. In practical terms, you mark a variable with UPROPERTY(Replicated) and then register it in GetLifetimeReplicatedProps so the engine knows to send it. A concrete example is a player's CurrentHealth: the server changes it, and the engine sends that updated value to all clients who should see it. Unreal also supports RepNotify by using ReplicatedUsing to trigger an OnRep function on clients when a value arrives; this is useful for updating a HUD or local effects. A frequent misconception is that marking a variable as Replicated alone is sufficient—without adding it to GetLifetimeReplicatedProps the engine won't replicate it. Another subtlety is replication conditions, like COND_OwnerOnly, which let you limit who receives data — useful for private inventories or owner-only UI. Understanding replication gives you fine-grained control over bandwidth, privacy, and client experience. Remote Procedure Calls let you execute logic on a remote machine. There are three main types you must know. Server RPCs are called by a client and executed on the server; use them for input that must be validated and applied authoritatively, for example asking the server to apply damage. Client RPCs are called by the server and executed on a single owning client; they are ideal for client-specific feedback like showing a unique UI or playing a local sound. NetMulticast RPCs are called by the server and executed on all clients and the server itself — use them for global visual or audio effects, such as playing an explosion animation everyone should see.
